readerTitle: The nurse said yes. Why is there still no deal?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (병원 간호 근무표 소프트웨어, 호텔 조식용 베이커리) · 실제 기업·수치 없음
insight: 기관에 파는 일은 한 사람을 설득하는 일이 아니라, 거절할 수 있는 모든 사람의 걱정을 하나씩 덜어 주는 일이다.
misconception: 제품을 가장 좋아하는 실사용자가 '사겠다'고 하면 거래는 거의 끝난 것이다.

sources.text: B2B 구매 행동의 표준 개념 (구매 위원회, 구매자가 느끼는 위험)

factChecks.note: 병원 구매 절차(IT 보안 검토, 조달, 재무 승인 등)는 나라와 기관마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 특정 국가의 법·규정을 언급하지 않고 일반적인 역할만 적었습니다. 게시 전 '일반적 묘사'로 읽히는지 확인하세요.
수치나 통계는 사용하지 않았습니다. '수개월'처럼 기간을 표현한 부분이 과장으로 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.

cards.title: The nurse said yes. Why is there still no deal?
body: You sell an app that builds nurse shift schedules. A nurse manager at a city hospital tries the demo and lights up. "This would save me hours every week. We want it."
Months later, you're still waiting. Nobody said no. Nobody signed either.

image.label: A happy nurse manager holding a tablet, a long hallway of closed office doors behind her
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 앞쪽에 태블릿을 들고 웃는 간호 관리자, 뒤로 길게 이어진 복도에 닫힌 문 여러 개(문패: Finance, IT, Procurement). 실제 병원·회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: She wants it. What's your next move?
body: The nurse manager is keen, but she doesn't control the budget or the hospital's computer systems.
What do you do right after the great demo?

options.text: Send her the contract and ask her to push it through
options.feedback: It feels fast, but she can't sign alone. The contract lands on desks of people you've never met, with questions she can't answer.

options.text: Ask her who else must approve, and what each of them worries about
options.feedback: This is the **buying committee** at work. You trade a quick close for a map of every person who can stop the deal.

options.text: Offer a big discount if they sign this month
options.feedback: A deadline can create urgency, but price is rarely what's blocking a hospital. You give up margin without removing the real objections.

cards.title: One yes, many possible no's.
body: Each person judges the same app by a different question. Your champion only answers one of them.

breakdown.label: Nurse manager
breakdown.detail: Will this save my team time?

breakdown.label: Finance
breakdown.detail: Is it in this year's plan, and what does it cost over time?

breakdown.label: IT security
breakdown.detail: Is patient and staff data safe? Does it connect to our systems?

breakdown.label: Procurement
breakdown.detail: Does the contract meet our rules for suppliers?

breakdown.label: Head of nursing
breakdown.detail: Will staff accept it, and who is accountable if it fails?

cards.callout: Most of these people will never open the app.

cards.title: Buying committees: arm your champion.
body: In a **buying committee**, several people share the decision. Usually any one of them can block it, and none can approve it alone.
So your job changes. Instead of more demos for the nurse manager, give her what each colleague needs: a cost sheet for finance, a security summary for IT, standard contract terms for procurement.
She walks into each meeting with answers, not just enthusiasm.

image.label: A champion handing different folders to four colleagues
image.brief: 간호 관리자가 네 사람에게 서로 다른 색의 폴더를 건네는 장면. 폴더 라벨: "Cost", "Security", "Contract", "Rollout plan". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: IT asks the 3 a.m. question.
body: The IT security lead asks: "What happens if your system goes down at 3 a.m., right before a shift change?"
How do you answer?

options.text: Show your strong uptime record and say outages are rare
options.feedback: Evidence helps, but "rare" isn't "never." You answer how likely failure is, not what happens to her when it occurs.

options.text: Propose a pilot on one ward, an offline backup of each schedule, a named support contact and an easy exit
options.feedback: This is **risk in business buying**. You make a bad outcome small and survivable, so saying yes is no longer a gamble for her.

options.text: Ask the nurse manager to escalate to senior leaders and skip IT
options.feedback: You might save weeks. But you turn a careful reviewer into an opponent, and she still has a veto later.

cards.title: Risk: shrink the downside, not just the odds.
body: For a business buyer, a bad choice lands on them personally. If schedules vanish, it's the IT lead who explains why nurses didn't know their shifts.

People in that position often prefer the familiar option, even when yours is better. So lower what they could lose: start small, keep a fallback, offer references from similar hospitals, and make leaving easy.
The bigger the first step you ask for, the bigger the fear you must answer.

cards.title: Committees cost you time and money.
body: Selling this way is slow. Before you chase a hospital, check that you can afford months of meetings before the first payment.
Pilots need an end. Agree up front what success looks like and when the decision happens, or a free trial can drift on for a year.
And never promise safeguards you can't deliver. One broken promise to a risk-averse buyer can end the relationship.

cards.title: Now it's a bakery and a hotel group.
body: You bake pastries. The head chef at a hotel group tastes them and wants them for breakfast at all eight hotels. Purchasing and each hotel's manager must agree too.
What's your best next step?

options.text: Ask the chef to introduce you to purchasing, and offer a two-week trial at one hotel with a backup delivery plan
options.feedback: You use both ideas: the chef helps you reach the **committee**, and a small trial with a fallback lowers the **risk** of empty breakfast trays.

options.text: Cut your price so purchasing can't say no
options.feedback: Purchasing will like the price, but hotel managers worry about late deliveries, not cost. You lose margin and the main fear remains.

options.text: Go straight to the group's director with free samples for all eight hotels
options.feedback: It looks bold, but skipping the chef and purchasing can make them feel bypassed. A big first step also makes failure big.

cards.softwareNote: The hospital app and the bakery face the same two hurdles: several people who can say no, and a buyer who fears being blamed.

cards.title: Win every 'no' before you ask for the 'yes'.
body: You used two ideas. **Buying committees:** find everyone who can block the deal and give your champion an answer for each. **Risk in business buying:** make a bad outcome small with pilots, fallbacks and easy exits.
**Try it today:** pick one business customer you're chasing. List every person who could say no, and next to each name write the one thing they fear.
